summary: Presents the requirements and design for a Voucher Trading System. Vouchers represent a right to claim goods or services, as with loyalty points, digital coupons and gift certificates, and the system circulates them securely. It includes terminology, design principles and requirements.

eli5.summary: Think of gift cards and coupon points that can be handed around safely online. This note describes how a system for that could work.

questions: how to implement gift certificates online
subtitle: Requirements and design for a system to securely issue, trade, and redeem digital vouchers like gift certificates and loyalty points.

tldr.problem: Digital vouchers (gift certificates, coupons, loyalty points) need a unified system to prevent forgery, duplicate redemption, and unauthorized changes while supporting diverse voucher types from different issuers.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3506 defines a Voucher Trading System (VTS) model with four participant roles (issuer, holder, collector, provider) and three transaction types (issue, transfer, redemption), plus a Generic Voucher Language (GVL) to describe voucher properties.
tldr.outcome: VTS enables secure circulation of digital vouchers in e-commerce without requiring pre-established trust among participants, relying instead on trust in the issuer and the VTS provider.

today: RFC 3506 is an Informational document that outlined requirements and a design model for a Voucher Trading System and Generic Voucher Language. It has not been obsoleted. While no single unified VTS was standardized at the IETF, the RFC's conceptual model and terminology remain relevant for understanding digital voucher systems and e-commerce security.

sections.title: Background and Motivation
sections.content:
RFC 3506 addresses the challenge of handling digital vouchers in e-commerce. Loyalty points, coupons, gift certificates, and event tickets are common in physical commerce, and the Internet requires a standard way to handle them digitally. Without a unified system, each application would need its own voucher handling mechanism, driving up implementation costs and forcing users to maintain multiple software modules.

The RFC proposes a generalized Voucher Trading System (VTS) that treats all voucher types (points, coupons, certificates, tickets) uniformly using a common model and a generic description language. This uniform approach allows a single software module to handle diverse voucher types from multiple issuers securely.
sections.eli5: Online shopping uses digital versions of gift cards and coupons. Instead of building a different system for each store or coupon type, one system could handle them all safely.

sections.title: The Voucher Model
sections.content:
RFC 3506 defines a voucher as a 3-tuple (Issuer, Promise, Holder): an issuer who creates the voucher, a promise describing what the voucher entitles the holder to, and a holder who currently owns it. A voucher is formally a digital representation of the right to claim goods or services.

The VTS model involves four participant types: the issuer (creates vouchers), the holder or user (owns and transfers vouchers), the collector or examiner (redeems vouchers and fulfills the promise), and the VTS provider (guarantees that vouchers are not duplicated or reused improperly). Vouchers move through three transaction types: issue (issuer creates the initial voucher), transfer (holder passes ownership to a new holder by rewriting the holder field), and redemption (presentation shows the voucher without consuming it, or consumption deletes it from circulation).
sections.eli5: A voucher is who created it, what it promises, and who owns it now. Four kinds of people are involved: the creator, the owner, the person who accepts it, and the system operator. The voucher goes through three steps: creation, passing hands, and cashing in.

sections.title: VTS Requirements
sections.content: RFC 3496 organizes VTS requirements into three categories. First, diversity: the system must handle vouchers from multiple issuers and support many voucher types (points, certificates, coupons, tickets). Second, security: the system must prevent forgery (only issuers create valid vouchers), alteration (only the holder can transfer), duplicate redemption (vouchers cannot be cashed twice), reproduction (only one valid holder at a time), and must support non-repudiation and privacy of holder identity. Third, practicality: the system must be scalable (no single point of failure), efficient (fast redemption for high-volume use), and simple enough to implement and understand.
sections.eli5: The system must handle many types of vouchers from many creators, keep them safe from fakes and cheating, and be fast and simple to use.

sections.title: System Architecture
sections.content: RFC 3506 outlines three specifications needed to implement VTS. First, a Voucher Trading Protocol (VTP) for interoperability among different VTS implementations, though the RFC notes that standardizing a single protocol is impractical since vouchers may be stored in smart cards (offline decentralized), centralized databases (online), or other architectures depending on the voucher type. Second, a VTS Application Programming Interface (VTS-API) that encapsulates different VTS implementations behind a uniform interface, allowing applications to issue, transfer, and redeem vouchers without knowing the underlying mechanism. Third, a Generic Voucher Language (GVL) using XML to describe diverse voucher types and their properties in a uniform, interoperable way.
sections.eli5: To make this work, you need a way for different systems to talk to each other, a common programming interface for applications, and a language to describe what each voucher can do.

sections.title: The Generic Voucher Language (GVL)
sections.content:
The Generic Voucher Language (GVL) is an XML-based specification for describing voucher properties and behavior. GVL requirements include: semantics to control validity (when and how a voucher is invalidated on redemption), transferability (whether a voucher can be handed to another holder), circulation (who can issue or redeem it), and anonymity; syntax flexible enough to define application-specific properties (seat number, flight number, etc.); security parameters; efficiency for storage on devices with limited memory; and coordination with other standards like IOTP, XML-Signature, and ECML.

An example from the RFC shows a five-dollar discount coupon for a specific book described in GVL: it specifies the title, value, target merchandise (by ISBN), validity period (April 1, 2001 to March 31, 2002), and that one coupon must be spent to claim the discount.
sections.eli5: GVL is a language to write down what a voucher can do: what it's worth, what you can buy with it, when it expires, whether you can give it to someone else, and other rules.

sections.title: Application Scenarios
sections.content: RFC 3506 illustrates VTS with an e-commerce example: a consumer searches for goods, acquires a coupon (discount right) from an ad agency, acquires a gift certificate from a payment handler, transfers both to a merchant in exchange for an exchange ticket and loyalty points, and finally transfers the ticket to a deliverer in exchange for goods or services. The key insight is that participants do not need to trust each other; they need only to trust the issuer and the VTS provider. A merchant receiving an exchange ticket issued by another merchant can trust it because the issuing merchant is trusted and the VTS guarantees no duplication. This enables secure transactions among previously untrusted parties and provides privacy benefits (delivery handlers do not need the consumer's address; merchants do not need it either).
sections.eli5: You find something online, get a discount coupon, pay with a gift certificate, trade both to the store for a pickup ticket and reward points, then show the ticket to get the goods. Nobody needs to trust each other if they all trust the store that issued the ticket and the system that prevents fakes.
